Q84.t: A dark river coiling through a sea of lights
Q84.s: Find the Thames and London falls into place: a brown ribbon looping east through an enormous grey-green sprawl, then widening towards the North Sea. The M25 motorway draws a rough ring around it all. The Romans bridged the river here almost two thousand years ago, and the city has spread outward from that crossing ever since.
Q84.w: The looping Thames running east to its estuary; square reservoirs glint beside Heathrow on the western edge.
f: The M25 ring motorway is about 188 km long; at night it traces a faint loop of lights around the city.
The Thames is tidal right through London: in the centre the water rises and falls by several metres twice a day.
The Romans founded Londinium on the north bank of the Thames around AD 50.

q.q: What was London called in Roman times?

Q406.t: One city, two continents, one blue thread between them
Q406.s: Look for a thin blue line cutting a vast city in two: the Bosphorus, with Europe on one bank and Asia on the other. The Golden Horn curls into the old town on the European side. As Constantinople, this was an imperial capital for more than a thousand years.
Q406.w: A narrow strait running north–south between the Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara.
f: The Bosphorus is about 30 km long and well under a kilometre wide at its narrowest.
Three suspension bridges cross the strait; from cruise they show as fine pale lines.
At night the two shores glow as one ribbon of light along the water.

q.q: Which strait splits Istanbul between Europe and Asia?

Q3692.t: A grid of lights dropped into the Arabian desert
Q3692.s: Riyadh sits close to the middle of the Arabian Peninsula, hundreds of kilometres from any sea. From above it is a vast beige grid of broad avenues, edged on the west by the green thread of Wadi Hanifa. Its name comes from the Arabic for 'gardens' — the oases this valley once watered.
Q3692.w: A huge rectangular street grid in brown desert, with the long Tuwaiq escarpment running north–south to the west.
f: The Tuwaiq escarpment west of the city curves for roughly 800 km across central Arabia.
On Riyadh's north-western edge, the mud-brick At-Turaif district of Diriyah is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
The city stands about 600 metres above sea level on the Najd plateau.

q.q: What does the name Riyadh mean in Arabic?

Q5465.t: A flat-topped mountain near the tip of Africa
Q5465.s: Look for a mountain sliced flat like a table, with the city curled around its feet and the sea on both sides. South of it, a rocky finger of land runs down to the Cape of Good Hope. On many summer days a white cloud spills over the summit like a tablecloth, then melts away on the way down.
Q5465.w: A flat grey mountain block above a curved bay, a rocky peninsula running south, and a low island out in the bay.
f: Table Mountain's flat summit reaches about 1,085 metres — roughly a tenth of your cruising height.
The low island in Table Bay is Robben Island, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1999.
Cape Town is South Africa's oldest city, founded in 1652 as a supply station for Dutch ships.

q.q: In which year did the Dutch East India Company found Cape Town?

Q649.t: Rings within rings, like a cut tree trunk
Q649.s: Moscow is laid out like a tree trunk seen in cross-section: ring roads nested one inside another around the old centre, with radial highways running out like spokes. At night the whole pattern glows amber and white. Through it winds the Moskva River in big, lazy loops. The city first appears in a chronicle in 1147.
Q649.w: Concentric road rings with straight spokes radiating out; the winding Moskva River crosses the centre from north-west to south-east.
f: The MKAD, Moscow's outer ring motorway, is about 109 km long.
The inner Garden Ring runs for about 16 km around the historic centre.
The city and its river share one name: in Russian, both are called Moskva.

q.q: In which year is Moscow first mentioned in a chronicle?

Q8673.t: A megacity stitched together across a lagoon
Q8673.s: Lagos is as much water as land. Look for a broad lagoon behind a long, straight Atlantic beach, with the city spilling over the islands and shores all around it. A thin bridge strides across the water for kilometres. Portuguese sailors named the place after these lakes, and today it is one of Africa's largest cities.
Q8673.w: A wide brown-grey lagoon behind a ruler-straight surf coast, dense city on its islands and a long bridge across the water.
f: The Third Mainland Bridge runs about 11.8 km across Lagos Lagoon, linking the islands to the mainland.
Lagos was Nigeria's capital until 1991, when the government moved to Abuja.
In Yoruba, the city's own name is Eko.

q.q: What does the name Lagos mean in Portuguese?

Q220.t: The Eternal City, framed by old volcanoes
Q220.s: Rome lies about 25 km inland on the Tiber, which snakes through the centre in tight bends. A motorway ring, the Grande Raccordo Anulare, loops around the city. Look beyond it: the round lakes to the north-west and south-east fill the craters of extinct volcanoes. Tradition dates the city's founding to 753 BC.
Q220.w: A sprawl on a winding river, framed by the round crater lakes of Bracciano to the north-west and the Alban Hills to the south-east.
f: The Grande Raccordo Anulare ring road is about 68 km long.
Vatican City, the world's smallest country, lies entirely inside Rome.
Lake Bracciano, north-west of the city, fills an old volcanic basin about 9 km across.

q.q: Which river flows through Rome?

Q3870.t: A highland capital with lions on its doorstep
Q3870.s: Nairobi sits on a high plateau at about 1,800 metres, just east of the Great Rift Valley. It began in 1899 as a depot on the railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria, and its name comes from a Maasai phrase for 'cool water'. On its southern edge, open grassland is a national park where lions and giraffes roam within sight of town.
Q3870.w: A dense city with an open tawny plain — the national park — on its southern side; the Ngong Hills rise to the south-west.
f: Nairobi National Park begins only about 7 km from the city centre.
West of the city the land drops sharply into the Great Rift Valley.
The city lies less than 150 km south of the equator, yet its altitude keeps nights cool.

q.q: What does the Maasai name behind 'Nairobi' mean?

Q85.t: Where the green Nile valley opens into the delta
Q85.s: Cairo marks the hinge of Egypt. South of the city the Nile runs in a narrow green strip through desert; just to the north it fans out into the delta. The city fills both banks, with the Giza plateau and its pyramids on the western edge, where the houses stop and the Sahara begins.
Q85.w: A huge grey-beige city on the Nile, exactly where the thin green valley widens into the triangle of the delta.
f: Cairo was founded as al-Qahira, 'the Victorious', by the Fatimid dynasty in 969.
The line between irrigated fields and bare desert around Cairo is razor-sharp, even from cruise height.
The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for more than 3,800 years.

q.q: Which dynasty founded Cairo in 969?

Q90.t: An oval city inside a ring, with a river in loops
Q90.s: Paris proper is compact: a neat oval held inside the Boulevard Périphérique, with suburbs sprawling far beyond it. The Seine enters from the south-east, curves through the centre past two small islands, then leaves in a series of great loops towards the Channel. The Romans called the settlement Lutetia.
Q90.w: An oval ring road enclosing the dense centre, with the Seine snaking through it and meandering west in big loops.
f: The Boulevard Périphérique is about 35 km long and follows the line of the city's 19th-century fortifications.
Inside the ring, Paris covers only about 105 km².
The city began on the Île de la Cité, the larger of the two islands in the Seine.

q.q: About how long is the Boulevard Périphérique around Paris?

Q1899.t: Green hills on one bank, flat plain on the other
Q1899.s: The Dnipro splits Kyiv in two, and its banks could hardly differ more: steep wooded hills on the west, where the old city grew, and low flat land to the east. Sandy islands and side channels lie between them. Upstream, the river swells into a long reservoir. A thousand years ago this was the capital of Kyivan Rus.
Q1899.w: A broad river with sandy islands running north–south; the hilly old city on the west bank, newer districts on the flat east bank.
f: Just north of the city the Dnipro widens into the Kyiv Reservoir, more than 100 km long.
The Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, a cave monastery founded in 1051, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Large wooded islands in the Dnipro, such as Trukhaniv, sit right opposite the city centre.

q.q: Which river flows through Kyiv?

Q612.t: A palm tree drawn on the sea in sand
Q612.s: Few cities are so easy to spot. Off Dubai's coast, a palm tree has been drawn on the sea in sand, its fronds ringed by a crescent breakwater. Further out, a scatter of islets imitates a map of the world. Onshore, towers line the coast for kilometres, and the old town hugs a winding creek.
Q612.w: The palm-shaped island off a straight desert coast, with the cluster of 'World' islands further out to sea.
f: Palm Jumeirah was built from sand dredged from the sea floor and is roughly 5 km across.
The World islands are an archipelago of about 300 artificial islands laid out like a world map.
Dubai Creek, a natural inlet, was the heart of the old pearling and trading town.

q.q: What shape is Dubai's best-known artificial island?

Q2807.t: A capital on a high plateau, with snowy peaks behind
Q2807.s: Madrid lies almost at the centre of Spain, on a dry plateau more than 600 metres above the sea. Look for ring motorways drawing ever wider loops around it, and for the Sierra de Guadarrama to the north-west, often white-capped in winter. Philip II moved his royal court to this small town in 1561.
Q2807.w: A dense city on a tan plateau ringed by motorways, with the Guadarrama mountains rising to the north-west.
f: At about 650 metres, Madrid is the highest capital city in the European Union.
The Puerta del Sol in the centre is Kilometre Zero for Spain's radial national roads.
The city's own river, the Manzanares, is so small it barely shows from the air.

q.q: Which mountains rise north-west of Madrid?

Q71.t: Where the Rhône slips out of a crescent lake
Q71.s: Geneva sits at the south-western tip of Lake Geneva, where the Rhône leaves the lake and heads for France. The city is almost surrounded by French territory. On a clear day look south-east to the snowy Mont Blanc massif, and north-west to the long, dark wall of the Jura.
Q71.w: The narrow pointed end of a large crescent-shaped lake, with a river leaving it; the Jura ridge lies to the north-west.
f: The canton of Geneva shares about 100 km of border with France and only a few kilometres with the rest of Switzerland.
Underground, just west of the city, CERN's particle accelerator runs in a 27 km ring beneath the French border.
Lake Geneva is about 73 km long, curving like a crescent between Switzerland and France.

q.q: Which river flows out of Lake Geneva at Geneva?

Q1754.t: A city on islands where a lake meets the sea
Q1754.s: Stockholm is spread over fourteen islands at the point where Lake Mälaren drains into the Baltic. From above it is a jigsaw of water, granite and dark pine forest. To the east the archipelago takes over: tens of thousands of islands and skerries scattered towards the open sea. The city is first recorded in 1252.
Q1754.w: A jigsaw of islands and channels between a big lake to the west and a vast archipelago spreading east to the Baltic.
f: The Stockholm archipelago contains roughly 30,000 islands, islets and rocks.
Lake Mälaren sits slightly higher than the Baltic, and its water drains out through the city's channels.
The land here is still rising after the last Ice Age, by around half a centimetre a year.

q.q: About how many islands make up the Stockholm archipelago?

Q3718.t: The westernmost city of mainland Africa
Q3718.s: Dakar crowns the Cap-Vert peninsula, a hook of land pushing out into the Atlantic, the farthest west that mainland Africa reaches. From above, the city fills the whole triangle, with sea on three sides and the ochre Sahel behind. Just offshore lies the small island of Gorée, a UNESCO site and memorial to the Atlantic slave trade.
Q3718.w: A triangular peninsula jutting west into the Atlantic, built over almost entirely, with a small island off its south-eastern shore.
f: Pointe des Almadies, on Dakar's peninsula, is the westernmost point of mainland Africa.
Two low volcanic hills, the Mamelles, rise near the western shore; one carries a lighthouse.
Gorée Island became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1978.

q.q: Dakar stands on which peninsula?

Q34647.t: A city built on gold, its old mine dumps in view
Q34647.s: Johannesburg exists because of gold. It sprang up in 1886, after a rich reef was found along the Witwatersrand, a long east–west ridge on the high veld. Look along the city's southern side for flat-topped yellowish mounds — old mine dumps — strung out in a line that traces the reef buried below.
Q34647.w: A sprawling city on a high grassy plateau; a line of pale yellow mine dumps runs east–west along its south.
f: Johannesburg lies about 1,750 metres above sea level.
Witwatersrand means 'ridge of white waters' in Afrikaans.
Some Witwatersrand gold mines reach about 4 km below the surface, among the deepest in the world.

q.q: Which discovery led to the founding of Johannesburg in 1886?

Q727.t: A canal city on land won from the water
Q727.s: Amsterdam grew from a 13th-century dam on the river Amstel, and water still shapes everything you see: the broad IJ channel along its north side, the grey expanse of the Markermeer to the east, and a flat patchwork of polders all around. Many of those green rectangles lie below sea level.
Q727.w: Flat green polders cut by straight ditches, the city on a broad channel, and a large grey lake to its east.
f: Schiphol airport lies about 3 metres below sea level, on the bed of a lake drained in the mid-1800s.
The ring of 17th-century canals became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2010.
The North Sea Canal, opened in 1876, links the city's harbour with the sea about 25 km to the west.

q.q: Which river gave Amsterdam its name?

Q7903.t: A white city strung along the Atlantic surf
Q7903.s: Casablanca stretches along a flat Atlantic shore, a pale spread of buildings pressed right up to the surf line. Look for the long breakwaters of its port, one of the largest in Africa, curving out to sea. The name is Spanish for 'white house', echoing the Arabic Dar al-Bayda, and from the air the city does look mostly white.
Q7903.w: A pale city along a straight Atlantic coast, with a big harbour enclosed by long breakwaters.
f: The minaret of the Hassan II Mosque, on the seafront, is about 210 metres tall.
Part of the Hassan II Mosque stands on a platform built out over the Atlantic.
Casablanca is Morocco's largest city, though the capital is Rabat, about 90 km up the coast.

q.q: What does the name Casablanca mean?

Q64.t: A flat city of lakes, forests and one big green void
Q64.s: Berlin spreads across a flat, sandy plain left behind by Ice Age glaciers, and water is everywhere: the Spree winding through the centre, a chain of Havel lakes in the west, the broad Müggelsee in the east. Dark pine forests reach deep into the city. Look too for a vast open rectangle south of the centre — Tempelhof, an airport turned park.
Q64.w: A huge flat city scattered with lakes and dark forest; a large open green rectangle lies just south of the centre.
f: The A10 Berliner Ring motorway around the city is about 196 km long, one of Europe's longest ring roads.
Tempelhofer Feld, the old Tempelhof airport, is now an open park of about 300 hectares.
Berlin covers about 890 km², more than eight times the area of Paris inside its ring road.

q.q: Which river flows through the centre of Berlin?

Q3838.t: Two capitals facing each other across a great river
Q3838.s: Kinshasa lies on the south bank of the Congo, where the river spreads into a vast, lake-like pool dotted with sandy islands. On the far bank is Brazzaville, the capital of another country. Just downstream, the river leaves the pool and plunges into a long run of rapids. Henry Morton Stanley set up a trading post here in 1881 and named it Léopoldville.
Q3838.w: A sprawling city on the south shore of a broad, island-studded widening of the Congo River, with another city on the opposite bank.
f: Apart from Rome and the Vatican, Kinshasa and Brazzaville are the world's closest pair of capital cities.
Pool Malebo, the river's widening here, is about 35 km long and more than 20 km wide.
Below the city, the Livingstone Falls — a chain of rapids — lower the Congo by about 270 metres.

q.q: Which capital faces Kinshasa across the Congo River?

Q1524.t: A white city poured into a basin down to the sea
Q1524.s: Athens pours across a basin ringed by bare mountains, spilling down to the Saronic Gulf at the port of Piraeus. From above it is an almost unbroken white-and-beige carpet. Look at the mountain to the north-east: pale scars on its flanks are marble quarries, worked since antiquity, when they supplied the stone for the Parthenon.
Q1524.w: A dense white city in a mountain-rimmed basin opening south-west onto the sea, with ship wakes fanning out from Piraeus.
f: The Parthenon's marble came from Mount Penteli, about 15 km north-east of the Acropolis.
Piraeus has served as the port of Athens since the 5th century BC, when the Long Walls linked the two.
The city takes its name from the goddess Athena, its patron in Greek myth.

q.q: Which mountain supplied the marble for the Parthenon?

Q1530.t: A city threaded on the loops of the Tigris
Q1530.s: Baghdad is threaded on the Tigris, which swings through it in great looping bends, with dark palm groves along both banks. To the west the Euphrates comes within a few dozen kilometres: the two rivers of Mesopotamia draw closer here than almost anywhere else. The Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founded the city in 762 as a perfectly round walled town.
Q1530.w: A flat, dust-coloured city on a wide, deeply looping river, with dark green palm groves along its banks.
f: Al-Mansur named his new round city Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace.
Near Baghdad the Tigris and the Euphrates run less than 50 km apart.
In the 9th century Baghdad's House of Wisdom drew scholars who translated Greek science into Arabic.

q.q: Which river flows through Baghdad?

Q3624.t: A capital in the clouds, ringed by eucalyptus hills
Q3624.s: Addis Ababa sits on the Ethiopian Highlands at about 2,350 metres, one of the highest capitals in the world. The hills to its north are dark with eucalyptus, a tree brought in during the 1890s to give the young city firewood. Emperor Menelik II and Empress Taytu founded the city in 1886, near a group of hot springs.
Q3624.w: A sprawling city on a high green plateau, with dark eucalyptus-covered hills rising along its northern edge.
f: The African Union has its headquarters in Addis Ababa.
The eucalyptus around the city came from Australia and now covers much of the Entoto hills.
At this altitude water boils at about 92 °C rather than 100 °C.

q.q: What does the name Addis Ababa mean in Amharic?

Q3616.t: A city tilting down from a wall of mountains
Q3616.s: Tehran lies at the foot of the Alborz, a steep mountain wall that shuts the city off from the Caspian Sea to the north. The whole city tilts: its northern districts sit hundreds of metres higher than the southern ones, which fade into dry plain. To the north-east, look for a lone white cone above the range — Damavand, the highest peak in Iran.
Q3616.w: A huge grey city pressed against a high mountain wall to its north; a lone snowy volcanic cone stands out to the north-east.
f: Mount Damavand, about 70 km north-east of the city, reaches roughly 5,600 metres.
Tehran became the capital in 1786 under Agha Mohammad Khan, founder of the Qajar dynasty.
Damavand is a volcano, and the highest in Asia.

q.q: Which volcano rises north-east of Tehran?

Q1741.t: Where the Danube runs in straight parallel lines
Q1741.s: Vienna's river is easy to find but strange to look at: the Danube passes the city in straight parallel channels with a long, thin island between them. That is the work of engineers; the old river once wandered freely across its floodplain. To the west, the wooded hills of the Vienna Woods are the last foothills of the Alps.
Q1741.w: The Danube as two straight parallel channels with a slim island between them, north-east of the centre; forested hills to the west.
f: Danube Island, the thin strip between the channels, is about 21 km long and was built for flood protection.
Vienna has working vineyards inside its city limits, and wine-making here goes back centuries.
For centuries Vienna was the main seat of the Habsburg dynasty.

q.q: Which river flows through Vienna?

Q3640.t: A capital on the bare steppe of Anatolia
Q3640.s: Ankara spreads over a bowl of hills in the middle of the Anatolian plateau, nearly 900 metres up and ringed by dry, tawny steppe. Its old name, Angora, lives on in the soft wool of goats, cats and rabbits once bred here. Far to the south you may catch a gleam of white: Lake Tuz, a vast, shallow salt lake.
Q3640.w: A large city in a bowl of low hills on bare, tan steppe; far to the south, the white sheet of a salt lake.
f: Ankara replaced Istanbul as Turkey's capital in 1923.
In Roman times the city was Ancyra, capital of the province of Galatia.
Lake Tuz is so shallow that in summer much of it dries into a crust of white salt.

q.q: Which old name of Ankara was given to a soft wool?

Q1781.t: Buda's hills and Pest's plain, stitched by bridges
Q1781.s: The Danube runs straight north to south through Budapest and splits it into two characters: the wooded hills of Buda on the west bank and the flat, dense grid of Pest on the east. A slim, leafy island, Margaret Island, sits in mid-river near the centre. The towns on the two banks were only merged into one city in 1873.
Q1781.w: A broad river flowing south, green hills on its west bank, flat city to the east, and a narrow island in mid-stream.
f: Budapest sits on a geological fault that feeds more than a hundred thermal springs.
South of the city the Danube splits around Csepel Island, which is nearly 50 km long.
Margaret Island is about 2.5 km long and once held a medieval convent.

q.q: In which year were Buda, Óbuda and Pest united?

Q2471.t: An ancient capital on a high mountain plateau
Q2471.s: Sanaa lies in a high basin among the mountains of Yemen, at about 2,250 metres. From above it is an earth-coloured patch between bare, folded ridges. Its old city, packed with tall tower houses of mud brick and stone trimmed in white, has been inhabited for more than 2,500 years.
Q2471.w: An earth-toned city in a broad upland basin, hemmed in by bare, rugged mountains on its east and west.
f: The Old City of Sanaa has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1986.
West of the city rises Jabal an-Nabi Shu'ayb, at about 3,660 m the highest peak in the Arabian Peninsula.
Sanaa's tower houses are several storeys tall, with white gypsum friezes framing their windows.

q.q: Roughly how high above sea level is Sanaa?

Q1492.t: A perfect grid between the hills and the sea
Q1492.s: Barcelona fills a coastal plain boxed in by two rivers and a line of wooded hills. Its heart is unmistakable: the Eixample, a vast chessboard of near-identical blocks laid out in the 1860s. Look for one broad avenue slicing across it at an angle, and for the hill of Montjuïc rising straight up from the port.
Q1492.w: A grid of square blocks between green hills and the Mediterranean, crossed by a long diagonal avenue, with a rounded hill by the port.
f: The Eixample was planned in 1859 by the engineer Ildefons Cerdà.
Each Eixample block is about 113 metres across, with its corners cut off at an angle.
The Avinguda Diagonal cuts across the grid for about 11 km.

q.q: Which hill rises beside Barcelona's port?

Q19660.t: A flat city with a string of lakes along its north
Q19660.s: Bucharest lies on the flat Wallachian plain, about 60 km north of the Danube. Look along its northern side for a chain of lakes strung along the little Colentina river, like beads on a thread. The first document to mention the city was signed here in 1459 by Vlad III — better known as Vlad the Impaler.
Q19660.w: A large, flat city on an open plain, with a curving chain of small lakes along its northern edge.
f: Its elegant boulevards once earned Bucharest the nickname 'Little Paris'.
Bucharest became the capital of Wallachia in 1659.
The Dâmbovița river crosses the centre in a straight, walled channel.

q.q: Which ruler signed the first document naming Bucharest, in 1459?

Q41183.t: One of the world's oldest cities, on a limestone plain
Q41183.s: Aleppo is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth, a stop on caravan routes between the Mediterranean and Mesopotamia for thousands of years. From above it is a large pale city on a rolling limestone plain. Its old centre grew up around a citadel on an ancient mound. South-east of the city lies a shallow salt lake, Jabbul.
Q41183.w: A large pale city on a dry, rolling plain; a shallow salt lake glints to the south-east.
f: The Ancient City of Aleppo has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1986.
The city has long been famous for soap made with olive and laurel oil, known worldwide as Aleppo soap.
Aleppo lies roughly 100 km inland from the Mediterranean.

q.q: Which salt lake lies south-east of Aleppo?

Q3766.t: An ancient oasis city beneath a bare mountain
Q3766.s: Damascus owes its existence to one small river. The Barada flows down from the Anti-Lebanon mountains and spreads into the Ghouta, an oasis of orchards that has fed the city for thousands of years. The city lies at the foot of bare Mount Qasioun, and in winter the snowy ridge of Mount Hermon stands out to the south-west.
Q3766.w: A large city between green orchards and desert, backed by a bare mountain on its north-west side.
f: From 661 to 750 Damascus was the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate, which stretched from Spain to Central Asia.
Mount Hermon, south-west of the city, rises to about 2,800 metres and often keeps snow into spring.
The Ancient City of Damascus has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1979.

q.q: Which fabric takes its name from Damascus?

Q72.t: A city at the end of a long, slender lake
Q72.s: Zürich sits at the northern tip of Lake Zurich, a slim lake that curves about 40 km south-east towards the Alps. The river Limmat drains out of it straight through the centre. On a clear day, look past the lake to the snowy wall of the Glarus Alps. The Romans knew the settlement as Turicum.
Q72.w: The northern end of a long, narrow lake curving south-east, a river leaving it through the city, and the Alps beyond.
f: Lake Zurich is about 40 km long but nowhere more than about 4 km wide.
The Uetliberg, the wooded ridge on the city's western edge, rises to about 870 metres.
Zürich is Switzerland's largest city, although the federal government sits in Bern.

q.q: Which river flows out of Lake Zurich through the city?

Q597.t: Mainland Europe's westernmost capital, on a wide estuary
Q597.s: Lisbon climbs its hills on the north shore of the Tagus, just where the river's broad inland lake narrows into a channel to the Atlantic. Two long bridges cross the water: a red suspension bridge at the narrows and, upstream, a thin line of a bridge that runs on for kilometres. No capital in mainland Europe lies further west.
Q597.w: A hilly city on the north shore of a broad estuary, with a long bridge across its upper reaches and another at the narrows.
f: The Vasco da Gama Bridge across the Tagus is about 12 km long, one of the longest in Europe.
The inland part of the estuary is so wide that locals call it the Mar da Palha, the 'Sea of Straw'.
Cabo da Roca, west of Lisbon, is the westernmost point of mainland Europe.

q.q: Which river forms the broad estuary at Lisbon?

Q1963.t: Where the Blue Nile and the White Nile become one
Q1963.s: Khartoum stands at one of the great river meetings of the world. The Blue Nile, coming down from the Ethiopian Highlands, joins the White Nile, which has travelled all the way from Lake Victoria. Their waters can run side by side in two shades for a while before they mix. Around the confluence, three cities face each other across the rivers.
Q1963.w: Two large rivers meeting in a Y around a green island, with a city on each of the three banks.
f: Tuti Island sits right at the confluence of the two Niles.
Most of the water in the Nile below Khartoum comes from the Blue Nile, especially in the flood season.
The three cities around the confluence are Khartoum, Omdurman and Khartoum North.

q.q: Which two rivers meet at Khartoum?
q.a: The Blue Nile and White Nile
x: The White Nile and the Sobat

Q374365.t: The Red Sea gateway, fringed by turquoise reefs
Q374365.s: Jeddah stretches for kilometres along the Red Sea, a long, narrow city pressed between desert and a band of turquoise shallows. Those pale greens and blues offshore are coral reefs. For centuries pilgrims bound for Mecca, about 70 km inland, have landed here, and the old port town grew rich on their arrival.
Q374365.w: A long city along a straight Red Sea coast, edged by bright turquoise reefs, with brown desert and hills behind.
f: Historic Jeddah, an old quarter of houses built from coral stone, became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2014.
King Fahd's Fountain, off the city's seafront, throws water more than 250 metres into the air.
The reefs along this coast are part of one of the warmest and saltiest seas on Earth.

q.q: Which sea does Jeddah face?

Q5806.t: A holy city in a valley of dark, bare mountains
Q5806.s: Mecca lies in narrow valleys among dark, jagged mountains, about 70 km inland from the Red Sea. For Muslims it is the holiest city of Islam: they turn towards it in prayer, and millions come each year on pilgrimage. East of the city, look for the Mina valley, carpeted with rows of white tents that house pilgrims during the Hajj.
Q5806.w: A city squeezed into winding valleys between bare black hills, with a valley of white tents stretching away to the east.
f: The Prophet Muhammad was born in Mecca around AD 570.
The tent city in Mina holds tens of thousands of fireproof tents in neat rows.
The plain of Arafat, a key stop of the pilgrimage, lies about 20 km south-east of the city.

q.q: What covers the valley of Mina, east of Mecca?

Q585.t: A capital at the end of a long, island-dotted fjord
Q585.s: Oslo sits at the head of the Oslofjord, where a long arm of the sea finally runs out between forested hills. The city fills a green amphitheatre, and dark woods scattered with lakes begin right at its edge. For three centuries it was called Christiania, after the Danish-Norwegian king Christian IV, who rebuilt it in 1624.
Q585.w: The inner end of a long fjord scattered with small islands, with the city in a bowl of dark, forested hills.
f: The Oslofjord runs about 100 km from the city south to the Skagerrak.
The city took back its medieval name, Oslo, in 1925.
Much of the municipality is protected forest, the Marka, laced with lakes and ski trails.

q.q: What was Oslo called from 1624 until 1925?

Q5468.t: A warm harbour city on the Indian Ocean
Q5468.s: Durban wraps around a big natural harbour on South Africa's east coast, sheltered by a long, wooded ridge called the Bluff. North of the port, a straight line of beaches faces the Indian Ocean, where the warm Agulhas Current keeps the water mild all year. Inland, rolling green hills are patched with sugar-cane fields.
Q5468.w: A near-enclosed bay with a narrow entrance, a green ridge along its south side, and a long straight beach to the north.
f: The city was named in 1835 after Sir Benjamin D'Urban, then governor of the Cape Colony.
Durban's harbour is one of the busiest ports in Africa.
The warm Agulhas Current flows south-west along this coast, one of the fastest ocean currents on Earth.

q.q: Which ocean does Durban face?

Q656.t: Peter's city on the islands of the Neva delta
Q656.s: Saint Petersburg spreads over the islands of the Neva delta at the eastern tip of the Gulf of Finland. Look for a thin line crossing the gulf to the west: a barrier about 25 km long, running through Kotlin Island, that shields the city from storm surges. Peter the Great founded the city on this marshy ground in 1703.
Q656.w: A big city on a branching river delta at the head of a gulf, with a long dam crossing the water through an island.
f: The Neva is only about 74 km long, yet it drains Lake Ladoga, the largest lake in Europe.
The city is built on dozens of islands, divided by rivers and canals.
Around midsummer, the 'white nights' keep the sky light even at midnight.

q.q: In which year did Peter the Great found Saint Petersburg?

Q182984.t: An ancient Sahel trading city on the savanna
Q182984.s: Kano spreads across the flat, dusty savanna of northern Nigeria, a vast carpet of low, earth-coloured roofs. For a thousand years it has been a trading city, a southern end of the caravan routes across the Sahara. In its old walled heart, cloth is still dyed in pits of indigo that have been in use since the 15th century.
Q182984.w: A huge low city of sandy browns on flat, dry savanna, with green fields and reservoirs scattered around it.
f: The Kofar Mata dye pits have been worked for more than 500 years.
Kano's Kurmi Market dates back to the 15th century.
The rainy season here lasts only about four months, from June to September.

q.q: Which dye colours cloth in Kano's old dye pits?

Q270.t: A capital on a river still left half wild
Q270.s: Warsaw stands on the Vistula, and the river is the surprise: while most capitals have tamed theirs, here broad sandbanks, willow thickets and beaches line the water right through the city. The centre sits on a low escarpment on the west bank; the Praga district faces it across the river. The royal court moved here from Kraków around 1596.
Q270.w: A wide river with pale sandbanks and green, wooded banks winding north through a large city on a flat plain.
f: The Vistula, Poland's longest river, runs just over 1,000 km from the Carpathians to the Baltic.
Frédéric Chopin was born in 1810 at Żelazowa Wola, about 50 km west of Warsaw.
Warsaw's historic Old Town is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: From which city did Poland's royal court move to Warsaw around 1596?

Q1960.t: A 'haven of peace' on a sheltered harbour
Q1960.s: Dar es Salaam curls around a narrow, sheltered harbour on the Indian Ocean, with coral islets and turquoise reefs scattered just offshore. Sultan Majid of Zanzibar founded the town in the 1860s and gave it an Arabic name meaning 'haven of peace'. Today it is Tanzania's largest city, sprawling far inland across the coastal plain.
Q1960.w: A sprawling coastal city around a narrow-mouthed harbour, with small green islands and reefs just offshore to the north.
f: Tanzania's official capital is Dodoma, but Dar es Salaam remains its largest city and main port.
Zanzibar Town lies about 70 km to the north, across a channel of the Indian Ocean.
The islands just north of the city, such as Bongoyo and Mbudya, are part of a marine reserve.

q.q: What does the name Dar es Salaam mean?

Q1761.t: A river city between a round bay and green mountains
Q1761.s: Dublin rings the inner curve of Dublin Bay, with the Liffey running straight east through its heart into the sea. The rocky peninsula of Howth closes the bay to the north, and the Wicklow Mountains rise dark and green just to the south. Vikings set up a fortified harbour here in 841, beside a dark tidal pool — the dubh linn.
Q1761.w: A city around a rounded bay, a river running east through its centre, a knobbly peninsula to the north and hills to the south.
f: Phoenix Park, on the city's western side, covers about 700 hectares — one of Europe's largest enclosed city parks.
The city's Irish name, Baile Átha Cliath, means 'town of the hurdled ford'.
Two long sea walls reach into the bay from the river mouth; the southern one was finished in the 1790s.

q.q: What does 'dubh linn', the source of Dublin's name, mean?

Q3748.t: A rain-soaked capital on a green cape
Q3748.s: Monrovia stretches along Cape Mesurado, a narrow peninsula between the Atlantic and a maze of lagoons and mangrove creeks. It is one of the rainiest capitals on Earth, and in the wet season the land around it glows a deep green. The city was founded in 1822 by freed African Americans and named after US president James Monroe.
Q3748.w: A narrow cape between the ocean and a mangrove-fringed river mouth, with the city running along its spine.
f: Monrovia gets more than 4,500 mm of rain a year, several times as much as London.
The first settlers landed in 1822 on Providence Island, in the mouth of the Mesurado River.
The city's port lies on Bushrod Island, wrapped by the Saint Paul and Mesurado rivers.

q.q: Which US president was Monrovia named after?

Q2634.t: A city on a famous bay, beneath a volcano
Q2634.s: Naples curves around one of the most famous bays in the world, and its landmark is impossible to miss: the cone of Vesuvius, cradled in the broken rim of an older volcano just south-east of the city. To the west lies another volcanic area, the Phlegraean Fields, pitted with craters. Out in the bay float Capri and Ischia.
Q2634.w: A broad bay with a big volcanic cone on its south-eastern side, islands at its mouth, and the city along the north shore.
f: Vesuvius rises to about 1,280 metres straight from the shore of the bay.
The Phlegraean Fields west of the city form a large volcanic caldera, partly under the sea.
Greek settlers named the city Neapolis, and its historic centre is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: What does the Greek name Neapolis, Naples' origin, mean?

Q490.t: A flat city on the Po plain, the Alps on its horizon
Q490.s: Milan lies in the flat heart of the Po plain, a city of rings around a medieval core, with motorways and railways fanning out in every direction. Look north on a clear day: the Alps rise like a white wall, and at their feet glint the great lakes, Como and Maggiore. In late Roman times, as Mediolanum, this was an imperial capital.
Q490.w: A dense, roughly round city on a perfectly flat plain, with the Alps and long glacial lakes to the north.
f: Milan Cathedral was begun in 1386 and took nearly six centuries to finish.
With no big river of its own, Milan dug canals, the Navigli, from the 12th century to reach the Ticino and Adda.
On clear days Monte Rosa, more than 4,600 metres high, can be seen from the city.

q.q: What was Milan called in Roman times?

Q87.t: A long ribbon of a city between sea and lake
Q87.s: Alexandria stretches for kilometres along the Mediterranean, a thin ribbon of pale buildings squeezed between the sea and the shallow Lake Mariout behind it. Look for the curve of its eastern harbour. Alexander the Great founded the city in 331 BC, and its lighthouse, the Pharos, was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.
Q87.w: A narrow city strung along a straight coast, with a curved harbour and a flat lake and marshes just inland.
f: The city runs more than 30 km along the coast but is only a few kilometres deep.
The ancient Library of Alexandria was one of the great centres of learning of the classical world.
The Pharos stood on an island at the harbour mouth for well over 1,500 years.

q.q: Who founded Alexandria in 331 BC?

Q1794.t: A city on the Main, its airport carved from forest
Q1794.s: Frankfurt lies on the Main about 30 km before it joins the Rhine, with the dark, wooded Taunus hills rising to the north-west. South of the river a great forest spreads out, and cut into it is one of Europe's busiest airports, its runways pale stripes among the trees. For centuries this was where German kings were elected.
Q1794.w: A compact centre on a river running east–west, with a big forest to the south cut by long, straight airport runways.
f: From 1356 the Holy Roman Emperors were elected in Frankfurt, and from 1562 they were crowned here too.
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was born in Frankfurt in 1749.
The Taunus range to the north-west rises to about 880 metres at the Großer Feldberg.

q.q: Which river flows through Frankfurt?

Q1055.t: A great port far up the Elbe, with a lake at its heart
Q1055.s: Hamburg lies about 100 km up the Elbe from the North Sea, yet it is one of Europe's largest ports. From above, look for the maze of docks and container terminals on the south bank, and for a bright lake right in the city centre: the Alster, a small river dammed centuries ago. Hamburg was a leading city of the Hanseatic League.
Q1055.w: A wide river with a maze of harbour basins on its south bank and a broad lake in the city centre just north of it.
f: The Alster lakes were created in the Middle Ages by damming a small river to drive a mill.
The Speicherstadt, a warehouse district built on oak piles, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
The tide reaches Hamburg: here the Elbe rises and falls by more than three metres.

q.q: Which lake lies in the centre of Hamburg?

Q1726.t: A Bavarian city with the Alps on its doorstep
Q1726.s: Munich spreads across a flat gravel plain on the green Isar, with the wall of the Alps only about 60 km to the south. On clear days, especially when the warm, dry Föhn wind blows, the peaks look close enough to touch. South-west of the city, two big lakes, Starnberg and Ammersee, glint among fields and woods.
Q1726.w: A large city on a flat plain split by a green river valley, with lakes to the south-west and the Alps beyond.
f: Munich's name comes from the monks, 'Mönche', who lived here before Henry the Lion founded the town in 1158.
The first Oktoberfest was held in 1810 to celebrate a royal wedding.
At about 520 metres, Munich is one of the highest large cities in Germany.

q.q: Which river flows through Munich?

Q1085.t: A river bending in S-curves through a hundred spires
Q1085.s: The Vltava gives Prague its shape. From above, the river swings through the city in a broad S, with the wooded rise of Petřín and the castle ridge on the west bank and the dense old town on the east. Green islands sit in the stream. About 30 km further north, the Vltava ends its journey in the Elbe.
Q1085.w: A river making big S-shaped bends through a dense city, wooded hills on its west bank and small islands mid-stream.
f: Prague Castle is often listed as the largest ancient castle complex in the world.
Charles Bridge was begun in 1357 under Emperor Charles IV.
The historic centre of Prague has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1992.

q.q: Which river flows through Prague?

Q35178.t: A desert city curled around a wide, shallow bay
Q35178.s: Kuwait City wraps around the southern shore of Kuwait Bay, a broad inlet at the north-western corner of the Persian Gulf. Around it lies flat, almost featureless desert, crossed by ring roads that curve out from the old town in wide arcs. The name comes from the Arabic for 'little fort', and the town grew on pearling and seafaring.
Q35178.w: A city on the south shore of a wide bay, with semicircular ring roads arcing out into flat desert.
f: The city's ring roads, numbered First to Seventh, curve out from the old centre in concentric arcs.
On Failaka Island, at the mouth of the bay, stand the remains of a Greek temple from the 3rd century BC.
Before oil, pearl diving was the backbone of Kuwait's economy.

q.q: What does the name Kuwait mean?

Q3761.t: A capital right next door to the zero meridian
Q3761.s: Accra spreads along a flat stretch of the Gulf of Guinea, its low roofs running inland over a grassy coastal plain. Just to the east, at the port of Tema, the Greenwich meridian comes ashore, so you are very close to zero longitude — and only about 600 km north of the point where it crosses the equator.
Q3761.w: A broad, low city on a flat, gently curving coast, with a long ridge of hills rising inland to the north.
f: The Greenwich meridian passes through Tema, about 25 km east of central Accra.
Accra's name is thought to come from 'nkran', an Akan word for ants.
Accra became the capital of the British Gold Coast colony in 1877.

q.q: Which port near Accra lies on the Greenwich meridian?

Q3579.t: An old Mediterranean port between sea and desert
Q3579.s: Tripoli spreads along the Libyan coast, a pale city on a low shore where a belt of gardens and palm groves gives way inland to desert. Phoenicians founded it as Oea in the 7th century BC. Its Greek name means 'three cities', after Oea and its neighbours Sabratha and Leptis Magna, both now famous Roman ruins.
Q3579.w: A pale city on a straight Mediterranean shore, a harbour at its old centre, green farmland fading into desert behind.
f: The Arch of Marcus Aurelius, built around AD 165, still stands in Tripoli's old town.
Leptis Magna, some 120 km east of the city, is one of the best-preserved Roman cities in the Mediterranean.
Tripoli's walled old town sits right beside the harbour.

q.q: What does the Greek name Tripoli mean?

Q33935.t: A white city on the dunes, an ancient port at its tip
Q33935.s: Tel Aviv lines a straight, sandy stretch of the Mediterranean, a dense band of pale buildings pressed right up to the beach. At its southern end, on a low rocky headland, is Jaffa, a port used for thousands of years. Tel Aviv itself is young: it was founded on the dunes north of Jaffa in 1909.
Q33935.w: A pale, dense city along a ruler-straight sandy coast, a small headland at its southern end, a river mouth to the north.
f: Tel Aviv's 'White City' holds thousands of Bauhaus-style buildings and has been a UNESCO site since 2003.
The name Tel Aviv means 'spring hill' — spring as in the season.
The Yarkon River reaches the sea at the city's northern edge.

q.q: Which ancient port forms Tel Aviv's southern end?

Q1757.t: A granite peninsula city fringed with islands
Q1757.s: Helsinki sits on a ragged granite peninsula poking into the Gulf of Finland, surrounded by bays, inlets and more than three hundred islands. At the harbour mouth, a cluster of islets carries the old sea fortress of Suomenlinna. In a cold winter the sea around the city freezes, turning the whole archipelago white. Tallinn lies only about 80 km across the gulf.
Q1757.w: A rocky peninsula ragged with bays and islands, facing south across the gulf, with forest and lakes inland.
f: Helsinki became Finland's capital in 1812, taking over from Turku.
The Suomenlinna sea fortress, begun in 1748, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Helsinki is the northernmost capital in the European Union.

q.q: Which king founded Helsinki in 1550?

Q121157.t: A pilgrimage city in a valley between two ranges
Q121157.s: Mashhad fills a broad valley in north-eastern Iran, with the Binalud mountains to the south-west and the Hezar Masjed range to the north-east. It grew around the shrine of Imam Reza, and its name means 'place of martyrdom'. Millions of pilgrims arrive every year, making it one of the great pilgrimage centres of the Muslim world.
Q121157.w: A large city in a wide valley, between a high, often snowy range to the south-west and bare mountains to the north-east.
f: The tomb of Ferdowsi, author of the Persian epic Shahnameh, stands at Tus, about 25 km from the city.
Mashhad is Iran's second-largest city after Tehran.
The Binalud range south-west of the city rises above 3,000 metres.

q.q: Which poet's tomb stands at Tus, near Mashhad?

Q1748.t: Where a bridge dives into a tunnel under the sea
Q1748.s: Copenhagen faces the Øresund, the strait between Denmark and Sweden. Look south of the city for one of Europe's great engineering lines: a bridge runs out from Sweden, lands on an artificial island and then vanishes into a tunnel under the sea to reach the Danish shore. The city itself spreads over the edge of Zealand and the flat island of Amager.
Q1748.w: A long bridge crossing the strait to an artificial island, where it disappears; the city and airport lie on the Danish side.
f: The Øresund Bridge is about 8 km long, and the link continues in a 4 km tunnel under the sea.
Peberholm, where the bridge meets the tunnel, is an artificial island built for the crossing.
Bishop Absalon built a castle here around 1167, traditionally taken as the city's founding.

q.q: What does the Danish name København mean?

Q1515.t: A lagoon city with rainforest inside its limits
Q1515.s: Abidjan wraps around the Ébrié Lagoon, a long body of calm water behind a narrow sand bar on the Gulf of Guinea. The city's districts sit on peninsulas and islands, joined by bridges. Look for the straight cut through the sand bar — the Vridi Canal — that lets ships into the lagoon. Within the city, a block of dark green is protected rainforest.
Q1515.w: A city spread around a branching lagoon behind a straight sandy coast, cut through by a narrow canal to the sea.
f: The Vridi Canal, opened in 1950, turned Abidjan into one of West Africa's main ports.
Banco National Park, a remnant of rainforest, lies inside the city.
Abidjan is Côte d'Ivoire's largest city, though the official capital is Yamoussoukro.

q.q: Which lagoon does Abidjan surround?

Q239.t: A city whose river vanished beneath its streets
Q239.s: Brussels spreads over gentle hills in the middle of Belgium, ringed by a motorway and fading into farmland. Don't look for its river: in the 19th century the Senne was vaulted over and hidden beneath the boulevards. What you can see is the Sonian Forest on the south-eastern edge, a large dark block of old beech woods.
Q239.w: A large city in rolling farmland, circled by a ring motorway, with a big dark forest on its south-eastern edge.
f: The Sonian Forest covers more than 4,000 hectares, and parts of it are UNESCO-listed for their ancient beeches.
The Senne was covered over in the 1860s and 1870s and still flows in tunnels under the city.
The Grand-Place, the old market square, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: What does Bruocsella, the old name of Brussels, mean?

Q3897.t: A bay city sheltered by a long finger of sand
Q3897.s: Luanda curves around a bay on Angola's Atlantic coast, sheltered by the Ilha, a long, thin sand spit lined with beaches. Further south, another spit, the Mussulo peninsula, encloses a calm turquoise lagoon for kilometres. Portuguese settlers founded the city in 1576, making it one of the oldest European-founded cities south of the Sahara.
Q3897.w: A city curving around a bay closed by a thin sandy spit, with a longer spit and lagoon further south.
f: The Mussulo peninsula south of the city is a sand spit nearly 30 km long.
The cold Benguela Current keeps this coast surprisingly dry for the tropics.
The Kwanza River, which gave Angola's currency its name, reaches the sea some 70 km to the south.

q.q: Which European country founded Luanda in 1576?

Q3561.t: A white city stacked on the hills above a bay
Q3561.s: Algiers rises from a wide, curving bay in white tiers, climbing the steep hills behind the port; the French called it Alger la Blanche, 'Algiers the White'. Its Arabic name refers to small islets offshore, long ago joined to the mainland to form the harbour. The old Casbah clings to the slope above the sea.
Q3561.w: A white city climbing steep green hills around a broad, curving bay, with a long harbour breakwater.
f: The Casbah of Algiers has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1992.
The town was refounded in the 10th century by the Berber ruler Buluggin ibn Ziri, on the site of ancient Icosium.
Algeria is Africa's largest country by area, and Algiers is both its capital and largest city.

q.q: What does Algiers' Arabic name, al-Jazair, mean?

Q3792.t: A capital pressed right against a border
Q3792.s: Lomé lies on the Gulf of Guinea at the western end of Togo's short coastline, so close to Ghana that the city's edge runs straight into the border. Behind the straight, surf-washed beach, a chain of lagoons runs parallel to the coast. The town became the capital of German Togoland in 1897, and later of the independent country.
Q3792.w: A low city on a straight sandy coast with lagoons behind it and harbour breakwaters jutting out to sea.
f: Togo's entire coastline is only just over 50 km long.
Lomé's western districts run right up to the border with Ghana.
The city's Grand Marché is famous for its cloth traders, especially of printed wax fabrics.

q.q: Which country's border runs along Lomé's western edge?

Q3572.t: A city between two lakes, with Carthage next door
Q3572.s: Tunis lies on a narrow neck of land between two shallow lakes, where the Gulf of Tunis cuts deep into North Africa. East of the old town, the Lake of Tunis is split by a straight channel that lets ships through to the city's port. On the gulf's shore just to the north-east lie the ruins of Carthage, once Rome's great rival.
Q3572.w: A city between a shallow lagoon crossed by a straight channel to the east and a salt flat to the south-west.
f: The ruins of Carthage, some 15 km from the centre, have been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1979.
The Medina of Tunis, a maze of souks and alleys, is UNESCO-listed too.
The Lake of Tunis is only about a metre deep in places, and flamingos wade in its shallows.

q.q: Which ancient city's ruins lie beside Tunis?

Q7525.t: A city of deep bays near the tip of Crimea
Q7525.s: Sevastopol lies near the south-western tip of the Crimean peninsula, on a long, deep bay that cuts several kilometres inland, with smaller bays branching off it like fingers. Beyond the city, the land rises towards the Crimean Mountains. On a headland to the west are the ruins of Chersonesus, a Greek colony founded some 2,400 years ago.
Q7525.w: A long, narrow bay reaching inland from the Black Sea, with smaller side bays branching off and the city between them.
f: The main bay reaches about 7 km inland and is one of the best natural harbours on the Black Sea.
Chersonesus was founded by Greek colonists in the 5th century BC.
The modern city was founded in 1783.

q.q: Which ancient Greek city's ruins lie at Sevastopol?

Q1519.t: An island city in a maze of mangroves and shallows
Q1519.s: Abu Dhabi stands on an island just off the Gulf coast, separated from the mainland by a narrow channel and joined to it by bridges. Around it, the sea is a puzzle of turquoise shallows, sandbanks, dark mangroves and low islands. The city's central grid ends abruptly at the water, with a long corniche curving along its north-western shore.
Q1519.w: A grid-planned island city ringed by turquoise shallows, with dark mangroves and many low islands to its east.
f: Qasr al-Hosn, a fort that began as an 18th-century watchtower, is the oldest stone building in the city.
The emirate of Abu Dhabi covers more than four-fifths of the UAE's territory.
The mangroves east of the island are protected as a national park.

q.q: What does the name Abu Dhabi mean?

Q23438.t: A white capital between mountains and the Karakum
Q23438.s: Ashgabat lies on a narrow strip of green between two worlds: the bare Kopet Dag range rising to the south, and the Karakum Desert stretching away to the north. A thin line of water, the Karakum Canal, curves along the desert's edge, carrying water from the Amu Darya far to the east. The city is known for its white marble facades.
Q23438.w: A pale city at the foot of a bare mountain range, with sand desert to the north and a long canal curving past.
f: The Karakum Canal runs for more than 1,000 km across the desert, one of the longest irrigation canals in the world.
The ruins of Nisa, an early capital of the Parthians, lie just west of the city and are UNESCO-listed.
The Kopet Dag, south of the city, forms Turkmenistan's border with Iran.

q.q: Which desert stretches north of Ashgabat?

Q3881.t: A plateau capital that began at a railway siding
Q3881.s: Lusaka lies on a broad, flat plateau in the middle of Zambia, about 1,280 metres up, where the air is fresher than the latitude suggests. It grew from a small siding on the railway line from the south, built in the early 1900s. In 1935 it became the colonial capital, chosen for its central position and healthy altitude.
Q3881.w: A spreading low city on a flat, lightly wooded plateau, with farmland and red-brown earth all around.
f: The city takes its name from Lusaaka, a local headman whose village stood here.
The Kafue River passes some 50 km south of the city.
Thanks to the altitude, winters here are mild and dry, with cool nights from May to August.

q.q: What made Lusaka grow in the early 1900s?

Q3921.t: A highveld capital among granite hills and jacarandas
Q3921.s: Harare spreads over the high grassland of northern Zimbabwe, about 1,500 metres above the sea, where rounded granite hills poke out of the plateau. South-west of the city, look for a winding lake: Lake Chivero, a reservoir on the Manyame River. In October, thousands of jacaranda trees along the avenues burst into purple flower.
Q3921.w: A sprawling city on a flat grassy plateau dotted with granite outcrops; a winding reservoir lies to the south-west.
f: Harare lies at about 1,490 metres, so its summers are warm rather than hot.
Lake Chivero, about 30 km south-west of the centre, supplies much of the city's water.
The first settlement grew beside the Kopje, a granite hill next to today's city centre.

q.q: What was Harare called until 1982?

Q193250.t: A city of wide streets near a land of granite domes
Q193250.s: Bulawayo sits on the dry, open plateau of south-western Zimbabwe, a neat grid of unusually broad streets. They were laid out wide enough, it is said, for a wagon pulled by a full span of oxen to turn around. About 35 km south rise the Matobo Hills, a wild landscape of bare granite domes and precariously balanced boulders.
Q193250.w: A grid-planned city on a dry, flat plateau, with rough country of bare granite hills to the south.
f: The Matobo Hills have been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2003, noted for their ancient rock paintings.
Bulawayo was the royal town of the Ndebele king Lobengula before the colonial city was laid out in 1894.
Bulawayo is Zimbabwe's second-largest city.

q.q: Which granite hills rise south of Bulawayo?

Q1764.t: The world's northernmost capital, named after steam
Q1764.s: Reykjavík lies on a low peninsula on the south shore of Faxaflói bay, with the long, flat-topped ridge of Mount Esja across the water. To the south-west, the Reykjanes peninsula is a dark sweep of lava fields, some of the youngest land in Europe. The first settler, Ingólfur Arnarson, is said to have arrived around 874 and named the bay after steam rising from hot springs.
Q1764.w: A low, compact city on a peninsula, a flat-topped mountain across the bay, and dark lava fields to the south-west.
f: Reykjavík is the northernmost capital of a sovereign country.
Nearly all homes in the city are heated with hot water from geothermal sources.
Mount Esja, across the bay, rises to about 900 metres.

q.q: What does the name Reykjavík mean?

Q4093.t: Scotland's biggest city, on the shipbuilding Clyde
Q4093.s: Glasgow spreads along the Clyde, a river that once built a large share of the world's ships. Downstream, the river widens into the long Firth of Clyde, scattered with islands. To the north the low, green Campsie Fells rise, and beyond them, some 30 km away, lies Loch Lomond, the largest lake by area in Great Britain.
Q4093.w: A large city on a river flowing west to a long, island-studded firth, with green hills and a big loch to the north-west.
f: Loch Lomond is the largest lake in Great Britain by surface area.
Glasgow's name is often said to come from Gaelic words meaning 'dear green place'.
Glasgow is Scotland's largest city, bigger than the capital, Edinburgh.

q.q: Which river flows through Glasgow?

Q3894.t: A city of hills on the shore of Africa's largest lake
Q3894.s: Kampala is built across a cluster of green hills just north of Lake Victoria, with the city filling the valleys in between. Its name comes from an old Luganda phrase for 'hill of the impala'. You are almost exactly on the equator here: the line runs only about 35 km south of the centre, across the lake.
Q3894.w: A green, hilly city spilling down to a ragged bay of a vast lake, with the Entebbe peninsula to the south-west.
f: Lake Victoria is the largest lake in Africa and the main source of the White Nile.
The Nile leaves Lake Victoria at Jinja, about 80 km east of Kampala.
The Kasubi Tombs, burial place of the kings of Buganda, are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: Which lake lies just south of Kampala?

Q131694.t: A port city built inside an old volcano
Q131694.s: Aden grew on a rugged volcanic peninsula on the Gulf of Aden, and its oldest district really does sit in a crater, ringed by the jagged walls of an extinct volcano. Across the harbour, the Little Aden peninsula is another old volcano. The deep, sheltered water between them made Aden one of the great ports on the sea route between Europe and India.
Q131694.w: Two dark volcanic peninsulas enclosing a wide natural harbour, with the city tucked into their bays and craters.
f: The ancient Tawila cisterns, cut into the crater wall, were built to catch the area's rare rain.
In 1839 Aden became a British coaling station for steamships sailing to India.
Jebel Shamsan, the highest point of the crater rim, rises to about 550 metres.

q.q: What is Aden's old town, Crater, built inside?

Q8717.t: The inland port that once ruled trade with the Americas
Q8717.s: Seville lies on the Guadalquivir some 80 km upriver from the sea, on a flat, sun-bleached plain of olive groves and farmland. Ocean-going ships once sailed right up to the city, and from 1503 it held the royal monopoly on trade with the Americas. Downstream, the river winds through the vast Doñana marshes towards the Atlantic.
Q8717.w: A large city on a flat plain beside a river, with a straight, canal-like channel and farmland stretching in every direction.
f: Seville has Spain's only inland river port.
Magellan's expedition, the first to sail around the world, set out from Seville in 1519.
Seville Cathedral is often called the largest Gothic cathedral in the world.

q.q: Which river flows through Seville?

Q204365.t: An old sultanate town among Sahel granite
Q204365.s: Zinder spreads across the dry Sahel of southern Niger, a low, sand-coloured town scattered among outcrops of bare granite. It was the seat of the Sultanate of Damagaram, which grew rich on caravans crossing the Sahara between Kano and the north. Its old walled quarter, the Birni, still surrounds the sultan's palace.
Q204365.w: A low, sandy town among bare rocky outcrops on flat, dry Sahel plains, with scattered fields around it.
f: The Sultanate of Damagaram made Zinder its capital in the 18th century.
The Nigerian city of Kano lies about 200 km to the south.
Zinder served as the capital of the French colony of Niger until 1926.

q.q: Which city replaced Zinder as Niger's capital in 1926?

Q3674.t: A Sahel capital on the great river Niger
Q3674.s: Niamey spreads along the left bank of the Niger, a broad brown river bordered by green strips of rice fields and gardens in an otherwise dusty land. Only a small village in the late 1800s, it became the colonial capital in 1926 and has grown fast ever since. East of the city, the scrubland is home to the last wild herd of West African giraffes.
Q3674.w: A city on a wide brown river flowing south-east, with green ribbons of fields along its banks and dry plateaus beyond.
f: The last wild West African giraffes live around Kouré, about 60 km south-east of Niamey.
The Niger, Africa's third-longest river, loops through the Sahel past the city.
Downstream lies W National Park, named after a W-shaped bend of the Niger.

q.q: Which river flows past Niamey?

Q208718.t: A young Red Sea harbour with coral reefs offshore
Q208718.s: Port Sudan lies on a flat, hot strip of Red Sea coast, where a deep, coral-fringed inlet makes a natural harbour. It is a young city, built in the early 1900s to replace the old port of Suakin, whose channel was too narrow for modern ships. Offshore, look for turquoise patches in the deep blue: reefs and atolls.
Q208718.w: A low city around a sheltered inlet on a straight desert coast, with turquoise reefs offshore and dry hills inland.
f: Sanganeb, an atoll about 25 km offshore, is a UNESCO-listed marine national park.
The Red Sea Hills behind the coastal plain rise to more than 2,000 metres.
Work on the new port began in 1905.

q.q: Which old port did Port Sudan replace as the main harbour?

Q3780.t: A city between green mountains and a great harbour
Q3780.s: Freetown clings to the northern tip of a mountainous peninsula, wedged between forested hills and the wide estuary of the Sierra Leone River. That estuary is one of the largest natural harbours in the world. Portuguese sailors named the peaks 'Serra Leoa', the lion mountains. The city was founded in 1792 as a home for freed Africans.
Q3780.w: A city squeezed between green, mountainous ridges and a very wide river estuary opening onto the Atlantic.
f: The highest hills of the Freetown Peninsula rise to nearly 900 metres.
Settlers from Nova Scotia, formerly enslaved Africans, founded the city in 1792.
The peninsula's rainforest is protected as the Western Area Peninsula National Park.

q.q: What does the name Sierra Leone mean?

Q320049.t: A mud-brick gateway to the Sahara
Q320049.s: Agadez is a sand-coloured oasis town at the southern edge of the Aïr Mountains, where the Sahel gives way to the Sahara. For centuries it was a crossroads for Tuareg caravans carrying salt and goods across the desert. Its skyline is marked by a mud-brick minaret bristling with wooden beams, first raised in the early 16th century.
Q320049.w: A small, earth-coloured town on flat sand, with the dark, rugged Aïr Mountains rising to the north and east.
f: The minaret of the Grand Mosque is about 27 metres tall, one of the tallest mud-brick structures in the world.
The historic centre of Agadez became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2013.
The Aïr Mountains north of the town rise to just over 2,000 metres.

q.q: What is Agadez's famous minaret built of?

Q851576.t: A savanna city below a volcanic massif
Q851576.s: Nyala lies in the rolling savanna of southern Darfur, beside a wide, sandy wadi that runs with water only in the rainy season. From above, the land is dotted with acacia and cultivated patches that turn green after the summer rains. To the north-west rise the Marra Mountains, a volcanic massif crowned by a great caldera.
Q851576.w: A spread-out town on flat, dotted savanna beside a broad sandy riverbed, with dark volcanic highlands far to the north-west.
f: Jebel Marra rises to about 3,000 metres, far above the surrounding plains.
Nyala is the largest city in the Darfur region.
Rain falls here mostly between June and September; the rest of the year is dry.

q.q: What lies inside the summit caldera of Jebel Marra, near Nyala?

Q276534.t: A river town on the red earth of the ironstone plateau
Q276534.s: Wau sits on the Jur River in the north-west of South Sudan, where wooded savanna on reddish ironstone soils stretches in every direction. In the rainy season the whole region turns a vivid green and the river swells. Its water flows on towards the Sudd, one of the largest wetlands in the world, before reaching the White Nile.
Q276534.w: A modest town on a winding river amid flat, wooded savanna, with patches of red earth showing through.
f: Wau is one of the largest cities in South Sudan.
The Jur feeds the Bahr el Ghazal, which meets the White Nile at Lake No.
The reddish soils around Wau belong to the ironstone plateau that covers much of western South Sudan.

q.q: Which river flows past Wau?

Q821321.t: A thin green thread of the Nile through the desert
Q821321.s: Dongola sits on the west bank of the Nile in northern Sudan, where the river's strip of date palms and fields is only a few kilometres wide and yellow desert presses in on both sides. From above it is the clearest picture of how the Nile makes life possible. Upstream, Old Dongola was once a medieval Nubian royal capital.
Q821321.w: A narrow ribbon of dark green along the Nile, with a small town on its west bank and bare desert on both sides.
f: Kerma, about 50 km downstream, was the centre of one of Africa's earliest kingdoms more than 4,000 years ago.
Between Khartoum and Egypt the Nile makes a huge S-shaped bend, and Dongola lies on its north-flowing stretch.
Rain is so rare here that some years pass with almost none.

q.q: Old Dongola was the capital of which medieval kingdom?

Q686813.t: A town at the foot of sudden granite towers
Q686813.s: Kassala lies on the flat plain of eastern Sudan, right at the foot of the Taka Mountains, a cluster of bare granite domes that shoot up abruptly from the land and are unmistakable from the air. The seasonal Gash River flows past the town and spreads into an inland delta of farms to the north. The Eritrean border lies just to the east.
Q686813.w: A cluster of steep, bare rock domes rising straight out of a flat plain, with a town and green orchards at their base.
f: The Taka Mountains rise several hundred metres straight up from the surrounding plain.
The Gash River flows only in the rainy season and fans out into an inland delta north of the town.
Orchards watered by the Gash make Kassala known across Sudan for its fruit.

q.q: What rises abruptly beside Kassala?

Q26087.t: An Arctic island city under the northern lights
Q26087.s: Tromsø sits mainly on a small island between steep, snow-streaked mountains and deep sounds, about 350 km north of the Arctic Circle. Bridges and tunnels tie it to the mainland. In midwinter the sun doesn't rise for weeks and the northern lights often dance overhead; in midsummer it doesn't set. Polar expeditions long set out from here.
Q26087.w: A small city on a low island in a narrow sound, ringed by steep, white-topped mountains and fjords.
f: The midnight sun shines here from about late May to late July.
During the polar night, from late November to mid-January, the sun stays below the horizon.
Tromsø lies under the auroral oval, one of the best places on Earth to see the northern lights.

q.q: Roughly how far north of the Arctic Circle is Tromsø?

Q25804.t: A Viking-age town cradled in a loop of river
Q25804.s: Trondheim sits on the south shore of the long Trondheimsfjord, where the river Nidelva curls around the old town in a tight loop, almost turning it into an island. King Olav Tryggvason founded the town in 997, and for centuries pilgrims came here to the shrine of Saint Olav. Look for the fjord's broad arm reaching far inland.
Q25804.w: A city on a long fjord, with a river curling round the compact old centre in a near-complete loop.
f: Nidaros Cathedral, built over Saint Olav's grave, is the northernmost medieval cathedral in the world.
The Trondheimsfjord is about 130 km long, one of Norway's longest fjords.
Warm Atlantic water keeps the fjord largely free of ice through the winter.

q.q: What was Trondheim's medieval name?

Q26793.t: A rainy port ringed by seven mountains
Q26793.s: Bergen sits on Norway's west coast between steep mountains and a maze of islands and fjords, so it is no surprise that it is one of Europe's rainiest cities. Look for a small harbour bay cutting into the centre, framed by mountains. For centuries this was a key Hanseatic trading port, shipping dried cod from the north across Europe.
Q26793.w: A city squeezed around a narrow harbour between steep mountains, with countless islands and fjords spreading out to sea.
f: Bergen gets roughly 2,250 mm of rain in an average year.
Bryggen, the old Hanseatic wharf, has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1979.
The Sognefjord, Norway's longest and deepest fjord, opens to the sea north of the city.

q.q: Which Hanseatic wharf is Bergen famous for?

Q990080.t: A deep-water bay on Mozambique's northern coast
Q990080.s: Nacala lies on the shore of a long, deep bay on Mozambique's northern coast, one of the finest natural harbours in East Africa. The water is deep enough for big ships to come close in without dredging. From above, look for a narrow-mouthed inlet reaching inland between green hills, with coral reefs along the ocean shore outside.
Q990080.w: A long, deep inlet reaching inland through a narrow mouth, with a town on its shore and green hills around.
f: Nacala's bay is often described as the deepest natural harbour on Africa's east coast.
A railway links Nacala's port with landlocked Malawi.
Coral reefs fringe the coast outside the bay.

q.q: Which UNESCO-listed island lies about 60 km south of Nacala?

Q37701.t: The judicial capital on the open Free State plains
Q37701.s: Bloemfontein sits in the middle of South Africa's high, flat grasslands, about 1,400 metres up, where a few rocky, flat-topped hills — koppies — break the horizon. It is one of the country's three capitals, home to the Supreme Court of Appeal. It is also where J. R. R. Tolkien was born, in 1892.
Q37701.w: A compact city on wide, flat, tawny grassland, with a few small flat-topped hills around its centre.
f: Naval Hill, in the middle of the city, is a small nature reserve with giraffes.
South Africa has three capitals: Pretoria, Cape Town and Bloemfontein.
The city was founded in 1846 as a British outpost beside a spring.

q.q: What does the name Bloemfontein mean?

Q3926.t: The jacaranda city between long rocky ridges
Q3926.s: Pretoria lies in valleys between long, parallel ridges running east–west, part of the Magaliesberg range, about 50 km north of Johannesburg. It is South Africa's executive capital. In October and November tens of thousands of jacaranda trees bloom along its streets, washing whole suburbs in purple. The city was founded in 1855 and named after Andries Pretorius.
Q3926.w: A city spread along valleys between long, straight east–west ridges, merging southwards into the Johannesburg sprawl.
f: Tswaing, a meteorite crater about 1.1 km across, lies some 40 km north-west of the city.
The rocks of the Magaliesberg are more than two billion years old.
Pretoria's jacarandas are not native: they were brought from South America.

q.q: Which tree turns Pretoria purple in spring?

Q80985.t: A medieval maze still living inside its walls
Q80985.s: Fez lies in a green valley between the Middle Atlas and the Rif, and its old medina, Fes el-Bali, is one of the largest car-free urban areas in the world. From above, it is a dense, pale mass in a bowl of hills, with the newer city laid out on the plain beside it. Its university, al-Qarawiyyin, dates back to 859.
Q80985.w: A dense, pale old city packed into a bowl of hills, with a grid-planned new town spreading beside it on the plain.
f: Al-Qarawiyyin, founded in 859, is often cited as the oldest continuously operating university in the world.
The Medina of Fez has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1981.
Fez's tanneries still dye leather in stone vats, much as they did centuries ago.

q.q: Who founded al-Qarawiyyin in Fez in 859?

Q3551.t: A capital facing its twin across a river mouth
Q3551.s: Rabat sits on the Atlantic where the Bou Regreg river reaches the sea, facing its older twin, Salé, across the estuary. On the clifftop at the river mouth stands the walled Kasbah of the Udayas. A little upstream, a 12th-century caliph began a vast mosque whose unfinished minaret, the Hassan Tower, still overlooks the water.
Q3551.w: Two cities facing each other across a river mouth on a straight Atlantic coast, with a walled fortress on the southern point.
f: The Hassan Tower was left unfinished when its builder, the Almohad caliph Yaqub al-Mansur, died in 1199.
Rabat's historic and modern city became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2012.
In the 17th century Salé was a base for Atlantic corsairs, the 'Sallee Rovers'.

q.q: Which city faces Rabat across the Bou Regreg river?

Q101625.t: A red city with snowy peaks on the horizon
Q101625.s: Marrakesh spreads across the flat Haouz plain, a city of ochre-red walls and palm groves. The view south is the show: the High Atlas rises like a wall some 50 km away, its peaks often white from winter into spring. Look for the dark green of the palm grove north of the city and the neat rectangles of old garden pools.
Q101625.w: A reddish city on a flat, dry plain, with a dark palm grove to the north and the snow-capped High Atlas to the south.
f: Toubkal, North Africa's highest peak at about 4,170 metres, lies some 60 km south of the city.
The Almoravid dynasty founded Marrakesh around 1070.
The Medina of Marrakesh has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1985.

q.q: Which mountain range rises south of Marrakesh?
